story.title: Goats Become Social Media Stars While Clearing Weeds in Tokyo
story.summary: Two white goats have gained popularity in Tokyo after being assigned to clear overgrown grass near Yotsuya railway station. Their eco-friendly efforts have attracted crowds of commuters and social media attention, turning them into local celebrities.

explore_lenses.label: Why use goats instead of mowers or herbicides?
explore_lenses.title: A low-mechanization weed-control trial
explore_lenses.summary: JR East is testing goats as an alternative way to manage vegetation on a small urban plot, rather than presenting them as a wholesale replacement for conventional maintenance. Grazing can reduce reliance on cutting equipment and herbicides, but it still requires animal care and may need to be combined with other controls depending on the vegetation goal.

claims.text: JR East's Yotsuya trial uses two goats on a 900-square-metre vacant plot as an alternative to conventional grass cutting and herbicides.

The Natural Resources Conservation Service says goat grazing can be used for vegetation management, while noting that combining biological control with mowing, herbicides or burning may be necessary for full elimination of unwanted plants.

University of Idaho Extension advises that weed-control grazing can require multi-year management and follow-up treatment, so the Yotsuya project alone cannot establish that goats will be sufficient for all future maintenance needs.

explore_lenses.uncertainty_note: JR East has not publicly released comparative cost, emissions, labor, or weed-removal results for this specific trial.

explore_lenses.label: Why was Yotsuya chosen for the trial?
explore_lenses.title: A controlled central-Tokyo test site
explore_lenses.summary: The location is notable because it is the first goat-grazing project inside Tokyo's Yamanote Line loop, where public visibility and railway safety make site control especially important. JR East says the plot was selected because its size, vegetation and ability to contain the goats met operational and safety conditions.

claims.text: The trial began on October 9, 2026, and is JR East's first goat-grazing project inside the Yamanote Line loop.

A JR East Ueno-area office representative said the site was chosen after considering weed-control effectiveness, management and safety, including whether the goats' movement could be appropriately controlled while protecting passengers and train operations.
JR East says station staff proposed the initiative and are responsible for the goats' day-to-day care, making this an operational trial rather than an unattended landscaping measure.

explore_lenses.label: Will the goats stay after December?
explore_lenses.title: This season is temporary; a return is planned
explore_lenses.summary: Nagi and Pokke are scheduled to work only until around December 2026, or earlier if they finish the available vegetation. JR East has indicated a possible spring 2027 return, but continuation remains contingent on operational results and site conditions.

claims.text: The current grazing period is expected to end around December 2026, unless the goats finish eating the vegetation sooner.
JR East's representative said the company has already observed some weed-removal effect and is using the operation to check both vegetation-control and management issues.
Forecast: JR East plans another grazing period from March through May 2027, according to its representative; this is a plan rather than a confirmed permanent program.

story_report.summary: Two goats are clearing overgrown vegetation near Tokyo's Yotsuya railway station in a JR East trial that has drawn crowds of commuters and made the animals popular on social media. The project uses grazing rather than conventional grass cutting and herbicides on a vacant plot, turning a routine maintenance task into a local attraction while the railway company assesses how well the approach works.

sections.heading: Yotsuya Grazing Trial Operations
sections.body: JR East began the trial on October 9, 2026, using two goats on a 900-square-metre vacant plot. It is the company's first goat-grazing project inside the Yamanote Line loop. A JR East representative said the location was selected after considering weed-control effectiveness, management and safety, including control of the goats' movement while protecting passengers and train operations. Station staff proposed the initiative and handle the animals' daily care.

sections.heading: Goat Grazing as Vegetation Control
sections.body: Goat grazing can be used for vegetation management, according to the Natural Resources Conservation Service, but it may need to be combined with mowing, herbicides or burning to fully eliminate unwanted plants. University of Idaho Extension likewise advises that weed-control grazing can require multi-year management and follow-up treatment. Those broader findings mean the Yotsuya trial alone cannot show that goats will meet all of the site's future maintenance needs.

sections.heading: JR East Plans Further Grazing
sections.body: The current grazing period is expected to end around December 2026, unless the goats finish the vegetation sooner. A JR East representative said the company has already observed some weed-removal effect and is examining both vegetation-control results and management issues. The representative said another grazing period is planned from March through May 2027, though that remains a plan rather than confirmation of a permanent program.

unresolved.text: JR East has not released comparative results for costs, emissions, labor or weed removal from the Yotsuya trial.
No independently published safety assessment or full animal-welfare protocol for the Yotsuya site was located.
JR East has not said whether it will make the program permanent, expand it to other central-Tokyo sites, or publish formal evaluation criteria.

related_stories.summary: An amateur cricketer known as 'Clicky Ponting' has been banned from cricket for two years due to cheating during matches. He was found to have been clicking his fingers while fielding to deceive the umpire into believing that the batsman had edged the ball.
